final_proof:
Let \(v_p\) be the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on \(\mathbb Q\), and let \(|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}\) for \(x\ne0\), with \(|0|_p=0\). Recall that \(\mathbb Q_p\) is the completion of \(\mathbb Q\) for this absolute value.

Let
\[
B=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N_0}
\]
be the set of all infinite binary sequences. For \(a=(a_0,a_1,\ldots)\in B\), define the integer partial sums
\[
s_N(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_np^n.
\]
If \(M>N\), then
\[
s_M(a)-s_N(a)=\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}a_np^n
\]
is divisible by \(p^{N+1}\). Therefore
\[
|s_M(a)-s_N(a)|_p\le p^{-(N+1)}.
\]
Since the right-hand side tends to \(0\) as \(N\to\infty\), \((s_N(a))_{N\ge0}\) is a \(p\)-adic Cauchy sequence. By the completeness of \(\mathbb Q_p\), it has a limit in \(\mathbb Q_p\). Thus we may define
\[
\Phi:B\longrightarrow\mathbb Q_p,\qquad
\Phi(a)=\lim_{N\to\infty}s_N(a).
\]

We claim that \(\Phi\) is injective. Let \(a,b\in B\) be distinct, and let \(k\) be the least index such that \(a_k\ne b_k\). For every \(N\ge k\), set
\[
D_N=s_N(a)-s_N(b).
\]
Because \(a_n=b_n\) for \(n<k\), we have
\[
D_N
=p^k\left((a_k-b_k)+p\sum_{n=k+1}^{N}(a_n-b_n)p^{\,n-k-1}\right).
\]
The integer in parentheses is congruent modulo \(p\) to \(a_k-b_k\), which is either \(1\) or \(-1\). It is consequently not divisible by \(p\), even when \(p=2\). Hence
\[
|D_N|_p=p^{-k}\qquad\text{for every }N\ge k.
\]
Also, \(D_N\to\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)\). Choose \(N\ge k\) sufficiently large that
\[
|(\Phi(a)-\Phi(b))-D_N|_p<p^{-k}.
\]
We use the elementary ultrametric fact that if \(|x-y|_p<|y|_p\), then \(|x|_p=|y|_p\). Indeed, the strong triangle inequality gives \(|x|_p\le |y|_p\); if this inequality were strict, applying the strong triangle inequality to \(y=(y-x)+x\) would give \(|y|_p<|y|_p\), a contradiction. Applying this fact with \(x=\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)\) and \(y=D_N\) yields
\[
|\Phi(a)-\Phi(b)|_p=|D_N|_p=p^{-k}>0.
\]
Thus \(\Phi(a)\ne\Phi(b)\), and \(\Phi\) is injective.

It remains to recall that \(B\) is uncountable. If its elements admitted an exhaustive list
\[
a^{(0)},a^{(1)},a^{(2)},\ldots,
\]
define \(c\in B\) by \(c_m=1-a^{(m)}_m\). For every \(m\), the sequence \(c\) differs from \(a^{(m)}\) in coordinate \(m\), so \(c\) is absent from the purported exhaustive list. This contradiction is Cantor's diagonal argument, and proves that \(B\) is uncountable.

Since the uncountable set \(B\) injects into \(\mathbb Q_p\), the set \(\mathbb Q_p\) is uncountable.
